EdgeCase is a Python package with a compiled Rust extension. It supports Python 3.9 and later on
macOS, Linux, and Windows.

## Installing from source

EdgeCase is not yet published on PyPI, so for now it is installed from its GitHub repository.
Building it compiles the Rust core, which needs a Rust toolchain. If you don't have one, install it
with [rustup](https://rustup.rs) first:

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

Then clone the repository and install the package. `pip` uses
[maturin](https://www.maturin.rs) behind the scenes to build the extension module:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase.git
cd edgecase
pip install -e .
```

The `-e` flag installs EdgeCase in editable mode, so changes to the Python sources take effect
without reinstalling. Changes to the Rust sources need a rebuild, which `maturin` does in place:

```bash
maturin develop --release
```

The `--release` flag turns on compiler optimizations. Leave it off for faster builds while working
on the Rust code, but use it for any benchmarking or for work on large graphs, since an unoptimized
build is many times slower.

## Dependencies

The core package needs only a few dependencies, which `pip` installs automatically:

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Polars](https://pola.rs) | The node and edge tables, Cypher query results, and step logs |
| [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) | Formatted summary tables |
| [anywidget](https://anywidget.dev) | Interactive graph widgets in notebooks |

Everything else is optional. EdgeCase imports an optional package only when you call a function
that needs it, and raises an `ImportError` naming the package if it isn't installed:

| Package | Needed for |
|---|---|
| [NetworkX](https://networkx.org) | `to_networkx()` and `from_networkx()` |
| [python-igraph](https://python.igraph.org) | `to_igraph()` and `from_igraph()` |
| [NumPy](https://numpy.org) | `to_numpy_array()` and `from_numpy_array()` |
| [SciPy](https://scipy.org) | sparse matrix conversion and Matrix Market files |
| [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org) | pandas edge lists and adjacency frames, and `steps.to_pandas()` |

The package defines extras that install groups of these:

```bash
pip install -e ".[networkx]"   # NetworkX
pip install -e ".[bio]"        # SciPy and scikit-learn
pip install -e ".[dev]"        # testing, linting and build tools
pip install -e ".[all]"        # all of the above, plus the documentation tools
```

## Verifying the installation

Once it is installed, import EdgeCase and print its version:

::: {#64c4a064 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import edgecase as ec

print(ec.__version__)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
0.1.0
```
:::
:::


A quick way to check that the compiled core is working is to build a small graph and run an
algorithm on it. This builds a cycle of five nodes and asks for the distance between two of them:

::: {#c65621c7 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=5).shortest_path_length(1, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2}
```
2
```
:::
:::


If that prints `2`, everything is in place. An `ImportError` that mentions `edgecase._core` means
the Rust extension wasn't built or was built for a different Python interpreter; running
`maturin develop` with the interpreter you are using fixes it.

## Development setup

To work on EdgeCase itself, the repository's `Makefile` wraps the common tasks:

```bash
make dev           # install with development dependencies, plus rustfmt and clippy
make build         # rebuild the Rust extension
make test          # run the Python test suite
make test-rust     # run the Rust unit tests
make lint          # run ruff and clippy
```

`make help` lists the rest, including benchmarks and coverage reports.
